html:
The release of cane toads in Queensland, Australia, in 1935, in the hope that they would eat beetles that were damaging the sugarcane crop. The toads ignored the beetles and spread across northern Australia, where they poison native animals.

The cane toad comes from Central and South America. In June 1935 the Bureau of Sugar Experiment Stations brought just over a hundred toads from Hawaii to Gordonvale, near Cairns, and soon released thousands of their young. The beetle larvae lived too deep among the cane roots and the toads could not reach them. But the toads bred fast, had no natural enemies, and moved steadily west and south. They crossed into the Northern Territory in the 1980s and reached Western Australia in the 2000s.

Glands on the toad's shoulders hold a strong poison. Quolls, goannas, snakes and freshwater crocodiles that try to eat them often die, and some local populations have crashed. The toads are now a textbook example of an invasive species brought in on purpose. Compare the rabbits released in 1859. See Australia.
